utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: First of all, I want to apologise for the late start, entirely my fault. And I've just been told now that you have been told five minutes' late start and I asked for a 15-minute late start because I knew I couldn't make it, so that makes two apologies. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Lisa Biersay, on behalf of the Prosecution, with Case Manager, Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your next witness is ready, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is ready, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, before the witness come in, I would just -- I would just inform the Chamber that we obtained the revised translation of the statement of DGH-199, and we would replace it with previous one. It is in e-court 1D113896 through 3890.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And was -- was that statement admitted? Is there an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, Your Honours. The exhibit number, I can't say it right now. I'll tell you it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So then it will be replaced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: First of all, thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. Secondly, I want to apologise for the late start. And now, then, could you tell us your name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sergija Veselinovic. 2nd of August, 1962.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalty of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could you now read the solemn declaration the Court Usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Although we know each other, I'll still introduce myself for the record. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I represent Goran Hadzic in these proceedings. Mr. Veselinovic, do you remember that you gave a statement, a written statement, to the Goran Hadzic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the copy of this statement for the witness and for Your Honours, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have, please, 1D3616 on the screen. It is tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have that statement in front of you? You have it on the screen and you also have it in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please go through the statement and see whether you can recognise your signature on each of the pages.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here in The Hague, while being prepared for this testimony, you made certain corrections and you added certain things to your statement. Therefore, I'm going to ask you to be so kind to look at the statement together with the rest of us. The first correction was made in paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at it and first tell me -- you said where you graduated. Did you want to correct that?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Obrovac and grammar school in Zadar. And then I continued studying at the Zadar university for three years, and then I completed my studies in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before you took your first employment, rather, before you started working in Zadar, did you work somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I worked at the archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Professor Marko Sunic [phoen], who was my professor, asked me to join him in translating some documents regarding a travel writer, Aleksander Diviling [phoen], and we also arranged the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Also in the first paragraph, you wanted to tell us something about the time when multi-party elections were held in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: That was in April 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, you spoke about the association of municipalities. You wanted to expand, and you wanted to tell us the regions from which those municipalities came.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Those were municipalities from Lika and Northern Dalmatia are mostly those municipalities in which the Serbian Democratic Party won the elections. Perhaps I could also add to that, that the association of municipalities of Zadar and Northern Dalmatia and Lika was set up because we were constantly obstructed by Zagreb and Split in trying to implement certain projects. The only way for us to protect ourselves was to set up our own association of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8, you mentioned an incident when Stevan Veselinovic and Dmitar Ceprnja were attacked. Where did that incident happen?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: That incident happened in the village of Pridreglija between Obrovac and Zadar, perhaps halfway between those two municipalities. The village was an ethnically pure Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12, you referred to the issuing of licences for hunting weapons. What hunting weapons did you have in mind when you said that licences were issued for them?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly for the conventional hunting carbine for big game.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 15, you stated the time up to which you served as president of Obrovac municipality. I believe that you wanted to make a correction there as well.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was not up to September but, rather, until May. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But that was in 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you please look at the following paragraph, paragraph 16. Again, there is a reference to September 1993. Do you think that you should make certain corrections in here as well?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the month would be May, not September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 18, you spoke about conflicts between Martic and Babic, and Babic's attempts to remove Martic from position. What period did you have in mind, and can you give us some more details of those happenings?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Babic was the prime minister of the RSK. At the same time, Martic was the minister of the interior. A conflict arose between the two of them. I believe that they didn't agree on the overall concept. They were at odds. And Babic removed Martic at a government session. However, after that, no single public security station accepted that. All chiefs, commanders, and police officers gave their full support to Martic who was an authority for the police. Babic appointed Dusan Vjestica to replace Martic. However, that decision was never implemented. It never took off the ground. In the field, Martic continued being the minister of the interior, even after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will kindly ask you to slow down so that your words may be correctly recorded. You mentioned the name of a man who was supposed to replace Martic. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Dusan Vjestica. Before he was appointed to that position by Babic, Dusan Vjestica was the president of the Executive Council of Gracac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just be very clear on the period. When was Babic prime minister or, rather, up to when was he prime minister?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Babic was prime minister until the moment the government was set up headed by Zdravko Zecevic, so we're talking April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure about April 1992? Perhaps you -- no, I won't -- I won't ask you anything there. In paragraph 22, you said that Croats were a majority in Zaton and Medvidja; those were local communes. I believe that you wanted to correct something there as well.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: In some parts or in some hamlets, they were a majority. They lived in groups in Modrici, Marici, Nekici [phoen], but they were not a majority in the entire local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, in paragraph 24, you wanted to give us an account of your movements around the time when you left the Republic of Serbian Krajina, i.e., when you arrived Belgrade, and when you decided to stay in Serbia for good. Could you please expand on that.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, every time there was an attack on the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and there were many such incidents, every time when we felt threatened, I would send my wife and my older son to Belgrade. That started in 1991 and lasted until 1993. I did that on several occasions. They left on several occasions. Our younger son was born in 1992, and that's when we would spend more time in Belgrade, a fortnight or even a month, because that younger child had some medical problems. We had to undergo physical therapy with him and rehabilitation. And as for our final decision to move to Belgrade for good and remain living there, we made that decision in October [Realtime transcript read in error "April"] 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the record, it says that you made that decision in "April 1993," the decision on your final departure to Belgrade. Not in your statement, but in the record. I believe that you mentioned a different month. Did you not? When did you finally decide to move to Belgrade? I believe that you're looking at the statement.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 24. But I believe that you --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: It was April. It was April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. I thought that you misspoke.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: It says September here, September 1993. That's when I left the Republic of Serbian Krajina and -- and I went to Belgrade with my wife and my older son. That's what I'm reading in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are having some little problems with the transcript now. Do you see that? We're no longer looking at the statement but at what is recorded in the transcript. It's on the screen, though you may not be able to understand it because it's in the English language?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was just about to tell you what it was about so that we clarify it. What is recorded here is that you said that you made the final decision to move to Belgrade in April 1993. A little while ago, you said that it reads there that you made the decision in September 1993. So for the sake of clarity, if you could tell us, if you remember, if you don't, you don't have to tell us exactly, but if you do remember, please tell us when did you make this decision to definitely move to Serbia and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we began discussing that option in April, but I don't remember the exact date when we definitely moved. Probably between April and September, we went to Belgrade at least three or four times and spent there 10 to 15 days each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, I will ask you if what is recorded in your statement with all the corrections that we have now entered and which are now on the record, whether all of that is truthful to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today as the ones on the basis of which you have given this statement, would you give essentially the same answers as recorded in the statement and as now corrected in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as corrected in the transcript right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask to admit -- I would admit -- I would tender this document into evidence. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, inter alia, in your statement, in paragraph 3, you talked about the secret arming of the Croats which took place before the outbreak of all the armed conflicts. This was done by the HDZ and the Croatian MUP. I wanted to ask you this: Where were you living at the time when all that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Zadar, in the Zadar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there many Serbs living in the Zadar municipality at the time?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what sort of impact did this have on the Serbs who were living there once they learned that the secret arming of the Croats was taking place?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: It was disastrous, especially the impact on the Serbs who lived in the urban centres --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the list of towns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was also because they believe that the past would be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, the interpreters asked for the witness to repeat the list of towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veselinovic, can you please list again, but slowly, the towns you mentioned a while ago.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: These were the Croatian urban centres where the Serbs were not the majority population but were, rather, in the minority but they worked there. Those were Sibenik, Zadar, Rijeka, Pula, Zagreb, Osijek, Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 10, you also talked about an incident in which a Croatian policeman was killed, Franko Lisica. You said that his colleagues organised the crystal night or "Kristallnacht" in Zagreb. Can you tell us what did you imply by this? What did actually happen?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: In a conflict between the National Guard Corps and the Krajina police, a member of the national Guard Corps or maybe the Croatian MUP was killed. His name was Franko Lisica. After that, the Croats organised the classical "Kristallnacht" in which they smashed all the Serbian restaurants, cafe and patisseries, companies from Serbia, shoe repair shops. Companies in question were Rad, Beko [phoen], Kluz [phoen], Novi Dom, the branch office of the Yugoslav air transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will interrupt you because you are speaking way too fast.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will not insist that you keep listing because this is sufficient. You also said that at the multi-party elections in Croatia in 1990 you were elected as president of the Obrovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether, in the territory of the Obrovac municipality, there were any Croats who lived there?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They made up around 25 per cent of the population, of the total population of this municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After you assumed your position, did they perhaps move out in the year when you came into power in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I object as to the leading nature of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question, but I don't believe that it is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened with the Croats after you assumed your position as the president of the municipality in 1990? I mean the Croats in Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: All the Croats who had worked in the municipal administration organs remained in their positions. None of the Croats who were employed in the territory of the Obrovac municipality was declared to be a technological surplus or was relieved of his duty or dismissed or demoted. The Croats remained in their positions, and the situation remained unchanged. It was as we found it when we assumed power. If I may also say, even though it wasn't like that in the municipalities where the HDZ won power. I know from personal experience that because my wife was employed in a municipal administration organ in Zadar, in the committee for agricultural. She had completed law studies and she was dismissed. My best man, Nikola Kosovic, who worked at the Secretariat of People's Defence in the Zadar municipality was also declared to be technological surplus and he was dismissed. I know many Serbs who have experienced the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the day when you came to the position of the president of Obrovac municipality, were there any movements of the Serbian population, whether out of the Obrovac municipality or into it?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs mostly arrived to the Obrovac municipality. The greatest number came from Rijeka and Zadar and a few were from the Sibenik municipality, because they were dismissed there. Their apartments had been taken away. The houses were torn down in a systematic manner, and so they would come to the territory of the Obrovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where these people were accommodated in the territory of the Obrovac municipality once they would arrive there?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: As the Obrovac municipality has 32 kilometres of the sea coast, it had many settlements and weekend cottages that were totally empty. It was out of season. These places would be full during the summer season. The owners would occupy them then. As we had so many people who had arrived to our territory, we had to provide for them. Our secretary of municipal administration, Jovo Vukcevic, made a plan, and he issued decisions. Of course, those were temporary decisions allowing them to use these facilities. All people who had moved into these houses had signed that they would return them in the same condition in which they were found with all the inventory. The inventory in the houses and weekends cottages was listed for each person who was issued such a decision and moved into this type of house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that every municipality had a Territorial Defence brigade. That's in paragraph 14. You also said that they were under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army. I'm interested in this: Did you, as the representative of the Obrovac municipality, have any jurisdiction over this Territorial Defence? Could you issue them any orders or anything of the kind?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The armed forces of Yugoslavia were comprised of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence was part of the federal organs. The municipality did not have any jurisdiction vis-a-vis the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as for the police, could you issue any orders to the police stations or specifically to the police station in Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That was also centralised at the republican level. They were responsible for their work to the Ministry of Interior in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about the period while the entire Yugoslavia still existed.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now asking you about the period when there were already the separations. Did you have any such responsibilities in that period or, in other words, could you command either the Territorial Defence or the police?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Neither. When there was an item on the agenda of the municipal assembly, that is to say, the security situation, I could invite a representative or chief of the police so that they would inform the municipal assembly about what was happening on the ground. But personally I had no jurisdiction whatsoever over the police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among Territorial Defence members - and I'm now talking about the period after the outbreak of the conflicts - among Territorial Defence members in Obrovac, were there any Croats?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Both in the police and in the Territorial Defence there was a proportionate number that corresponded to the ethnic composition of the population in the municipality. In other words, the answer is: Yes, there were ethnic Croats, both in the police and in the Territorial Defence throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when exactly did you join the government of Republika Srpska Krajina? When were you elected as a member of the government of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in April 1992, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D3763. It is tab 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the screen in front of you, on the left, you will see the list of salary payments, and we can see the people who held various positions listed there. That's the first column. The second column is a description of their positions. And the last column shows the date of their entry on duty. Under number 20, you will see your own name. It says that your position was that of a minister and the entry on duty is recorded as the 18th of May, 1992. Does that correspond and does that refresh your memory about the time --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it corresponds. It is possible that was when I received my first salary. Probably since the time I joined the government and the appointment at the session of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina which had to approve of the appointment, it's possible that this date is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I have no objection to that. But just to put on the record I believe that this is not on the Defence's 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is -- it is on Defence exhibit list -- oh. Yeah, yeah, yeah. You think about Rule 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It -- it might be -- it might be that it is not on -- on our list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It should be -- it should be, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it should be. However, I'd like to just to -- to add same document under the same number -- under -- the same document was admitted into evidence by the Prosecution. I cannot find right now -- right now the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could -- could the Registrar assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If you are sure, Mr. Zivanovic, that it is admitted as a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as P57.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then we don't have to admit it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I withdraw my request to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veselinovic, do you remember -- or, rather, let me ask you this: Were you ever a member of a government commission? Or, to be more precise, I'm going to ask you very specifically were you a member of a commission which was supposed to establish the situation in Gracac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was a commission. It had five members. I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1862. It is tab 8. May we see B/C/S page 9 and English page 12, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened in Gracac municipality to necessitate the establishment of a commission that was supposed to establish what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: A unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I remain open to be guided by my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic, but I -- I don't see anything indicating that the witness would be speaking about this issue regarding Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Generally, the witness was called to speak about the work of the government of RSK whose member he was. And it is a part of -- of the work of the -- in the government of RSK, and the Prosecution knows of the minutes from RSK government, and they're -- they're familiar with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think the fair question is whether or not the Prosecution was given notice that the witness would be discussing what I think he's been asked to do about situations on the ground in Gracac, and there's nothing in either the proofing note or his witness summary or, frankly, even in his statement that would indicate that this topic would be covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was what the witness has to do as a member of the government, as a member of the government related to the establishment of the -- establishment of the situation in the municipality of Gracac. It is a part of his -- his role in the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your question was, Mr. Zivanovic, what happened in Gracac municipality to necessitate the establishment of a commission. Isn't that a plain question about what happened on the ground in -- in -- in that municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I -- precise -- I'll clarify my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veselinovic, why was this commission set up? What was it supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The commission was set up because of an incident that happened in Gracac municipality. Members of our armed forces were on Mount Velebit very close to Sentros [phoen] and that was a point which was held by our armed forces. They were there during a truce and our unit was moving very peacefully in order to replace their colleagues on their positions, and the Croatian forces massacred 22 fighters of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I remember that among them there were four men who bore the same family name as me, Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: Was a truce in place or what?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the government ever received information and considered issues relative to the cutting off of the corridor leading to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The government did look at that issue, the issue of the corridor in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska. Actually, we're talking about three municipalities in the Sava valley. They were Modrica, Derventa, and Obuduvci, if I'm not mistaken. That route was a blood line for Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina. That corridor was used to transport medicines and all the other necessities. People travelled to Belgrade on that road. It was the throbbing way and the main artery, to use the lingo of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see the document from the Rule 65 ter list, Prosecution list, it is 1148; tab 32. [Interpretation] Let's look at page 2 in the original and in the English translation as well. I apologise. It will be page 3 in the English translation. I believe that it even spills over to page 4. Actually, it is page 4 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly look at bullet point 1. There's a report there on the cutting off of the corridor and the necessity to re-establish that corridor as soon as possible. Do you remember what Milan Martic said?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the government regarding that problem?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The government voiced a position and concluded that the opening up of the corridor is absolutely necessary and, in that sense, it authorised the minister of interior of Republic of Serbian Krajina, Milan Martic, and his assistant - I believe at that time it was Colonel Boro Djukic - to assign units which would participate in the operation to re-establish the corridor and ties with the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, do you remember anything about the relationship between the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, on the one hand, and the Yugoslav authorities, on the other hand, after the Vance Plan was signed in 1991? Were there any mutual obligations between the two?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, in contacts with representatives of the government of the Republic of Serbia and federal institutions, i.e., the authorities of Yugoslavia, we received very firm guarantees that the Republic of Serbian Krajina would never be abandoned at a session at which the Vance Plan was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, sorry for the interruption, but the previous document is said to be under seal in e-court. There is mention that it should be under seal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry for my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, gladly. On several occasions, the representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia persuaded us that we would not be left to our own devices and we would not be left at the mercy of Croatian armed forces. At a session of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Topusko, I remember there were five generals of the JNA, they, together with Professor Gavro Perazic, who was an international law expert, tried to convince us that in case of an aggression of -- by the Republic of Croatia against the Republic of Serbian Krajina that they would have an instrument, i.e., an iron fist, that be would able to respond within an hour and establish a separation line between the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Veselinovic, immediately after this event, when the cutting off of the corridor, did any armed action of the Croatian forces against the Republic of Serbian Krajina take place?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: There were several instances of aggression. The first one occurred at the Miljevci plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would stop there and then later on we would move on to the others. Could you tell us if the government discussed and examined the situation which arose due to the aggression on the Miljevci plateau?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: It did examine this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the government did? What sort of position did it take, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we mostly had objections to the work of the defence ministry. It seemed to us that everything was too slow and too complicated. They justified themselves by saying that our weapons were under the control of international forces, whereas the Croatian forces were completely free and could plan their actions. In such a skirmish as this, it was a significant advantage when you plan an action and you plan to surprise the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, Exhibit 1175 from the Prosecution list. It is tab 11. Do we have translation? I think there's translation of this document. No translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never mind. I won't ask you anything about this document because it seems there is no translation. Would you tell us what was the position taken at the time by the Yugoslav authorities, in view of the guarantees that you have told us about?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: They did not fulfil our requests, nor did they comply with the guarantees that had been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the position of the UNPROFOR at the time when that attack was launched? Was the UNPROFOR already deployed in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the UNPROFOR was there, present in the RSK. But after an operation, they would mostly just note the actual situation on the ground, and they no longer did anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, if you remember, whether during your tenure in the government when you attended the sessions whether Goran Hadzic attended any of these sessions?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this period of around a year and a half during which I was a member of the government, the RSK president, Goran Hadzic, came twice, just before the London Conference and once immediately after it, when he was the rapporteur. He reported to us about the negotiations that the Yugoslav delegation took part in, in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D2581.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd be greatly assisted by having a tab number, if possible. I think I found it. Is it tab 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Two, yes. May we see, please, page 2, both in B/C/S and English. [Interpretation] It seems to be on the following page, after all. No, no, no. [In English] That's okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If could you please look at item 1. It says here that the prime minister gave an introductory presentation and believed that that should be the platform for the work of the government. The concept is put forward to be used at the London Conference. Is that the session that you told us --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that the government adopted the conclusion to form a working group that would comprise the president of the republic, the prime minister, and some other ministers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that there were Dusan Ecimovic, David Rastovic, Nebojsa Mandinic, and Mile Dakic, master of arts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also remember whether after the London Conference Goran Hadzic reported to the government on the developments that took place at the conference?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: At the government session, which took place after London, Hadzic attended it and submitted a report. He talked in positive terms and said that this was the first time that at an international conference the name of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was heard and appeared. So he talked about the London Conference in very positive terms. He represented it as our chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you something about the work of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. You did say something about that in paragraph 17 of your statement. Inter alia, you mentioned that deputies of the Party for Democratic Changes were also members of the assembly. Can you tell us where was the seat of the Party of Democratic Changes?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Its seat was in Zagreb. There was another --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a little -- I'm sorry. Can you please tell us who was the president of that party?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Racan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the Social Democratic Party --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Party, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Social Democratic Party led by Zeljko Madjar [phoen] also had its deputies in the assembly. Can you tell us something more about this party and its leader?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The party itself was registered at the level of the Republic of Croatia. Its headquarters were in Rijeka. It was social democratic by orientation. Some of the Serbian voters voted for this political option.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Veselinovic, this is the time for our first break, 30 minutes. We will be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This morning you asked for the replacement of translation of a statement, a witness statement, and, on the record, it is witness statement of DGH-119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 099, I suppose it is. Is it Dafinic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 099. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And exhibit number is 199. D199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's on the record now. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the exhibit number is D --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit number is D199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And now we lift the MFI status; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to note that we are checking the translation and just to alert the Court that in the event we find something amiss, we'll take the issue up with the Court again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps. Perhaps we are a little bit too fast indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veselinovic, my next question is this: What was the influence of Goran Hadzic in Knin Krajina at the time and during the time you spent there?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Mr. Goran Hadzic spent very little time in our territory and that he did not have his own political party or headed a political -- an influential political party there, he had very little influence on the political processes which were happening in Krajina at the time. His influence was very small and limited, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who had a strong political influence in the Republic of Serbian Krajina at that time?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The two central political figures during that period of time were Milan Babic and Milan Martic. In an interview that I gave to the "Duga" magazine which is published in Belgrade, I spoke with journalist Zvonko Bogavac, and I told him that Mile Martic was the most important person there and that the influence of Milan Babic [as interpreted] in the government is really minimal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify something. Did you say that Milan Babic's influence in the government was minimal?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I said Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Wait till I finish my question. I'm going to read the entire sentence: [In English] "The two central political figures during that period of time were Milan Babic and Milan Martic. In an interview that I gave to the "Duga" magazine which is published in Belgrade, I spoke with journalist Zvonko ... and I told him that Mile Martic was the most important person there and that the influence of Milan Babic in the government is really minimal." [Interpretation] Did you say that or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No. The journalist was Zvonimir Bogavac and I said during that interview that Milan Martic was a real Gauleiter and that Goran Hadzic's influence and the government itself headed by President Zecevic was very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain the term "Gauleiter"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Gauleiter is a commissioner, a governor, a manager, a person of the highest authority in an area. This is a German word which dates back to the times of the Third Reich.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During 1992 and 1993 while you were in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, did the Croatian population move out of the area; to be more precise, from your municipality of Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, people did move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why? Why did people move out? Why did the Croatian population move out from that area?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: There was an incident in the village of Bruska. Two Croats were killed there as well as a Serb, and the last person, the Serb, was a postman. As a result, the Croats who lived in the area became seriously concerned for the first time. During that time, in my municipality, in two local communes where Croats were rather numerous, and those were Zaton near Obrovac and the village of Medvidja, on several occasions, I held meetings with representatives of the local Croats, i.e., the president of the local commune, the principal of the local elementary school, and the most reputable figures from the area. I begged them not to leave the territory of Krajina. My rationale for that was that the most important thing in life was to preserve one's own home. Since we were very mixed in the area, we were all related, we were all Kums, therefore, I -- I thought it was only good for them to stay in the area. And the second guiding motive was the fact that in Krajina, we had a pluralist society, and that we also had to have a minority population there. I believed that the best solution for the states which are multi-ethnic and multi-confessional was that, to have a minority. The second meeting that I held was in the clay factory in Obrovac, in the administrative building. I held a meeting there with the inhabitants of Zaton, a village near Obrovac. My proposal to them was the same and that was not to move out. I believe that my idea to talk to them was very much supported by an elderly man whose name was Modric and who had been a participant in the Second World War. He thought that that was a good thing that we should also send a police patrol that would patrol the area 24/7 and that they should stay in their homes. Unfortunately, some 20 days later, 20 days after the meetings that I've just mentioned, the civilian -- UNPROFOR police and the commander of the French Battalion, Colonel Meille, and also Lieutenant-Colonel Vladimir Kononenko, who was UNPROFOR CIVPOL, informed me that the Croats wanted to leave the territory after all, that they wanted to leave Obrovac municipality. And then, through the Red Cross and UNPROFOR bodies, the transfer of a certain number of Croats was arranged, and they left our municipality. I even remember a woman who worked in the administrative services of the municipality of Obrovac. She left her job, she left her house, and she moved to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, of the people who moved out, who left, how old were they? What was their age structure? Were they older, younger? Can you give us a rough idea.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about older people, older than 65. But there were also younger people among them as well. What was the problem, in my view? The families were divided. Some of them lived in Zadar, Zagreb, or Rijeka and the rest lived in our territory. Some of them expressed the desire to join up with their families, and, as for the rest, I suppose that they had economical reasons for wanting to move to Croatian side, because at that time we did not pay out salary. We did not have a pension fund. We did not have any funds for that matter. Whereas, at the same time, the Croatian state provided all that to their citizens. They were given accommodation in holiday homes. They have been given pensions. And all those who had worked in the administrative organs in Krajina, and I can talk specifically about Obrovac municipality, for example, that woman who left her job, when she moved to Zadar she was immediately given a job there because the Croats had established their own municipality of Obrovac which operated in the territory of the municipality of Zadar. So there was dual administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something else. You mentioned pensions. Could you tell us whether pensions were paid to those people who, before the war, before 1991, had been of pensionable age in Croatia? I apologise, I need to finish. In other words, those who had received regular pensions from the pension funds of the Republic of Croatia, after the war started, did they continue receiving pensions from the Croatian retirement fund who had paid their pensions up to then?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The Croats immediately stopped the payment of all pensions and any other benefits that the Serbs were entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were those payments stopped only to the Serbs or everybody who resided in the territory of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody. Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about those pensioners? What did they live on? Did they receive any monies at all? Since they lost their pensions, what did they live on, the aged and infirm?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them lived in rural areas. They grew their on produce, and we were also able to provide them with aid from the Red Cross. There was also a soup kitchen for anybody who could not feed themselves, could come to the soup kitchen and have at least one warm meal a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question: Those people who left Krajina, for example, those elderly people who were already pensioners, when they arrived Croatia, do you know if they continued receiving pensions?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as they crossed over to the Croatian territory, they were able to exercise all their rights. That's why I believe that was one the main reasons why they crossed over to the Croatian territory was that they were in -- better off financially or economically, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if either in Obrovac or elsewhere during that period of time while you were there in 1992 and 1993, were there any cases of forcible transfer of the Croatian population which was carried out in an organised manner?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were none. All the commands, the government, the Presidency ordered local structures to be very mindful and very considerate towards the Croats. It was very important for us to be different from them. The things that our fellow citizens experienced in Croatia or in the territory under the control of the Croatian government, we didn't want the same things to happen to ethnic Croats in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. We tried to protect them as much as we possibly could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said, inter alia, that there was a crime in Bruska when two Croats and a Serbian postman were killed. According to our information, that was not the only crime against Croats that happened in the Republic of Serbian Krajina during that time. Do you know if such crimes were investigated? Were perpetrators sought?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. When it comes to Bruska, as far as I know, that heinous act was motivated by financial gain. In the territory of the local commune of Medvidja there was also a number of murders --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. We'll come to that. My question is this: Were you in Obrovac when the Croatian forces launched the attack on Maslenica?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have a map, but it's not important. Can you tell us how far is Obrovac from the locations along the separation line and the places which came under the Croatian attack in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: The city itself was no more than 5- or 600 metres as the crow flies. We had a factory of hydroelectric cylinders there, the Djuro Djakovic factory, the Dalmatia bauxite mines, the stone quarry. All those were occupied by the Croatian forces. All that was part of our industrial zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And during those military operation do you know if Croatian troops committed crimes in that area in the territory of the municipality of Obrovac?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I interrupted you when you started talking about Medvidja. Can you come back to that and tell us what happened there. What happened in Medvidja?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: A man, Simon Sadaro [phoen], and his wife were killed. They were both Croats. After that, as far as I remember, a man called Erstic was also killed, and then Branko Genda was also killed. I can't remember any other crimes, but I assume there were other murders as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a Serb or Serbian people who were killed during the Maslenica operation?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: In the local commune of Zaton, which was very close to the industrial zone that were -- that was entered by the Croatian forces, three Serbian women were killed. I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1454. It is from Prosecution exhibit list, tab 22. It is not this exhibit, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think it was perhaps the P number that you were giving, not the 65 ter number, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is P1902. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to draw attention to the bottom part of the text where you will find a reference to the names and ethnic affiliations of the three woman whom you have mentioned. The site where those women's bodies were found is described. Is that the case that you referred to just a while ago --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- when you testified about the crimes?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the statement, it says that the statement was given by a man called Vuksic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him personally. He was an employee of the Secretariat of the Interior in Obrovac. I don't know what his name was. His nickname was Neno; he was a Croat. We followed the practice of sending Croats to the sites where an ethnic Croat had been killed because we wanted to avoid any suspicion of bias when it came to the work of our own police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina manage to repel the attack on Maslenica?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were your troops reinforced by troops from either Yugoslavia or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was a unit, a unit of the Volunteer Guards, and a small unit from the territory of Republika Srpska. I'm talking about the Wolves from Vucjak commanded by Veljko Milankovic, and the guards were headed by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. With the help of those forces, we managed to return some of the trigger points and the points that were of importance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first part of this report, if you can read it, one can see that events of the day are being reported on and towards the end of the first paragraph, the word is underlined. It says that: "The morale of our forces has significantly improved since Arkan came to this area." Would you tell me, first of all, whether it was so; and, if it was, how was the morale improved by his arrival?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: It's true. It's true that the morale was improved. So, firstly, any help coming from the side in such a difficult situation was God-given. It had a psychological impact. The population would be calmed down because perhaps more new forces would be expected. And, secondly, it was precisely those units that were able to counter-attack the enemy, and all of the actions carried out in the area of Tula Regrede [phoen] and Velebit. I'm talking about some villages at the foot of Mount Velebit. This was done by those units, Milankovic's and Arkan's units. Of our units, that part of the front was covered by the Light Obrovac Brigade, which was not trained to infiltrate enemy territory. We didn't have anyone expert for sabotage or navy infantry or any special units, and these guys were trained for that kind of a counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D3053. It is tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting for this document to appear on the screen, you also mentioned Milankovic and his units which had come from the Republic of Serbian Krajina. So I will ask you to look at a document which will appear on the screen just now, if you can tell us if that is what you were talking about. Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me whether this document portrays accurately what happened in the fighting with regard to these units.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it absolutely corresponds to the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D212, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me how these volunteer units which had arrived from other areas were received by Martic and Babic in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: In a very short period, after the arrival of this unit commanded by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, a conflict arose between him and the minister of the interior of the RSK, Milan Martic. Martic took measures. He refused to welcome them. I don't think that there was any use of force, but they withdrew from the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if, during the action at Maslenica, Goran Hadzic appeared in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: On one occasion. He stayed for about a week. We saw each other several times then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us something else. You have told us when you ceased to be a member of the government of the RSK, approximately. Could you also perhaps tell us some of the reasons why that happened?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Zecevic's government, Djordje Bjegovic became the RSK prime minister. He was a man who very often changes his political affiliations from Racan's SDP to the -- the League of Communists Movement for Yugoslavia. I refused to participate in such a government and to co-operate with a man of such political affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veselinovic, I will ask you another question; namely, if you could explain something a little. We talked about an incident which occurred in Krusevac in 1993, so if you could just very briefly tell us what happened in Krusevac in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that this was the most fatal incident in my life. It had to do with this: On the premises of the Society of Serbian Jewish Friendship, I met Aleksandar Andjelkovic. I was introduced to him through Enriko Josif, and Klara Mandic. After a while, I developed closer relations with him. Initially he was very favourably disposed to everything that was happening in the area of the Krajina. As he was living in Belgrade and had his private company and two business premises, one at the Sava Centre and the other one in Zmajinova Street close to the pedestrian zone of Knez Mihajlova Street. I had saved 7.000 Deutschemarks and 1700 Guilders, and I borrowed that money to Mr. Andjelkovic. He was to pay me back within a month. However, upon expiry of this period, I insisted on several occasions that he should pay me back the money that I had lent to him. I could see from his answers that he was going through some sort of financial problems. He would mention various people. Specifically I remember that he very often mentioned a Hungarian, Balint Pastor, who owned a company in Vrnjacka Banja and also a man in Krusevac from whom he expected to receive a large amount of money. They owed that money to him. He suggested that I come to Krusevac and see for myself that the man really owed him money which he could not pay back to me at the moment. So I went to Krusevac, and we met in the patio of a cafe restaurant in the very centre of the town. Sasa showed us for the first time the house where this man lived, but we didn't find him. The house was locked. During our second attempt, we found the man in front of the house. He told us to come inside and talk so we wouldn't talk in the street. As the man hailed from Kosovo, I suppose that that was part of the local culture: He suggested that we take our shoes off, which all the four of us did. We expected the arrival of this Mr. Andjelkovic who was in a car with a friend of his, Basic. However, they did not show up inside the house. One of the people who was there with us, and I hadn't known these people from before, that was the first time I saw them, took out a contract from his pocket and presented it to the owner of the house. He denied the validity of the contract or having any obligations towards anyone. All the while, I was sitting on the sofa together with this gentleman's wife and his mother-in-law. I asked them to fulfil their obligation and at least pay me back if they could do that anyway, even though they were not directly involved in the whole affair in which I had given the money. I remember that this Katanic and this Nikola whose last name I don't remember, went away twice with this Mr. Spasic, if I remember his last name properly, because it was a two-storey house. They would go upstairs, and after no more than five minutes, police showed up, and the three of us were arrested. At the moment, I did not know what happened with this Nikola and how he had disappeared. I later heard that he had left through the back garden and thus reached another street. I would like to note one very important thing. The weapons that I had on me at the time, it was a pistol produced by the Crvena Zastava factory from Kragujevac. I had a licence for it that was in order and I had crossed the border of the Republic of Serbia countless times with it. When asked by the border police if we had any weapons, every time we would answer in the affirmative. Sometimes they would check our licences; sometimes they didn't. My official driver at the time also had the licence. Sometimes there would be another man as my escort. He was also armed. We never had any problems as far as the Serbian police was concerned. As far as I remember, during the trial, I was charged with illegal possession of weapons. I believe that the sentence was three months. As far as I remember, the entire sentence was five or six months for the -- for the whole incident. On appeal, the sentence was changed and became a suspended one. I want to say that for the act itself, we did not have to serve any time in prison, neither I nor any of the other three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I shall not ask you anything else about this event. It will probably be a topic during the cross-examination later on. That was all I had. Those were all my questions. Thank you for the answers.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just forgot to tender the last document from the screen into evidence. It is 1D3053, tab 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It has been admitted as D212, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I may have one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, I see we're on the cusp of afternoon. Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Lisa Biersay. I will be asking you questions on behalf of the Prosecution today. I have been granted I believe four hours. And we'll see if we need that time. It depends on how efficient we are. Now, before I begin, I wondered if I was correct in noticing you silently greet Mr. Hadzic before you took the oath and he smiled back at you in acknowledgment. Do you recall that? Did you make a silent acknowledgment to Mr. Hadzic when you came into the courtroom and before you took the oath?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: When I saw him, I just nodded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And he --

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I may have smiled as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And he smiled at you; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And before the last -- the first break of the morning, you again acknowledged him and he again smiled at you; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that you and Mr. Hadzic are old friends.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I do put it that way. I want to know if you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The witness asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Veselinovic, you say that you first met Mr. Hadzic in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we have reference where the witness said that he first met Hadzic in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, let me ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When did you first meet Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I first met Mr. Hadzic in my office in the Obrovac municipality. He came there together with a professor of the faculty of law in Osijek, Vojislav Vukcevic. That was the first time we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you remember what year that was?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So just to recap, could you tell us exactly where you were living in 1991 for that year. Where -- where were you?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the Zadar municipality. That is where my father had his family house and that was where I was living. My wive lived there too, and so did my older son. I believed that I did say so at one point that my wife used to work in the administration organisation in the Zadar municipality in the committee --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... one moment. I just wanted to know where you were living and it's okay for the other details. And I believe that you've answered it. You lived in the Zadar municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in 1992, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: In Obrovac. In Obrovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in 1993, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Until May, if I'm not mistaken, in Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And then -- and then?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: And then in Belgrade. Occasionally in Belgrade. I still had not moved completely. I split my time between Belgrade and Obrovac, because you have to understand that moving one's family is a very complex thing and that it cannot be done overnight, not even within a month. It takes some time to start a new life, to find jobs, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And regarding your -- your duties, your political duties, were you still carrying those out in this period of transition, as you describe it?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, the "period of transition"? What time-frame would that be?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, I believe you described thinking about moving to Belgrade and then finally making the decision later on, in September, October 1993.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So between -- between May of 1993 and, let's say, October of 1993, were you still carrying out your -- your duties with the assembly, with the Obrovac assembly and also with the RSK government?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in the government and the assembly. I was a deputy in the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina during that period. After the fall of the government headed by Zecevic, I told you that my term of office finished. I didn't want to be a member of Djordje Bjegevic's government, and that government was established sometime in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say that you did not want to be a member of Djordje Bjegevic's government, how did you terminate your membership officially? Did you take any steps?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Under the Krajina laws, we were at disposal for six months. We were given six months to find new jobs and, in the meantime, we received regular salaries from the government. In other words, for the next six months on every first day of the month, we would still receive our dues.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how would they know not to give you your dues?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: That was regulated by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you spoke a lot with Mr. Zivanovic about various issues. You spent a lot of time talking about Krusevac. Krusevac is in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And am I correct that it's in the most eastern part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Southeastern. It would be in the south-east.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What I haven't really heard much about are your duties as minister of culture and religion. From -- during what periods did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: From April 1992, or thereabouts, until May, the beginning of May 1993, for approximately a year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And during that year, could you explain to the Trial Chamber what duties you exercised as the minister of culture and religion in the RSK government.

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did you do as minister of culture and religion?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Now I understand. You mean what my job description was? What my tasks were? As soon as I joined the ministry, we set up the state archives of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. We took certain measures to set up the state theatre of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I introduced religious education into the elementary and secondary school syllabus. I dealt with a number of issues within the sphere of culture, guest appearances, public gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we have some more information about the introduction of religious education into the elementary and secondary school syllabus of -- what was the nature of that religious education?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: In co-operation with the Ministry of Education and the then-minister was Milan Knezevic, we had to co-ordinate our activities in order to introduce religious education into elementary and secondary schools. We had to print textbooks. We had to define the issues that would be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say "issues," what do you mean? "Issues to be dealt with."

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: How shall I explain that? The work of the Ministry of Education entailed dealing with all the subjects: Biology, geography, foreign languages. They had to define what the children will learn, every day, and what issues will be covered within the syllabus, within the curriculum on each and every day when that subject was taught.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And so, if I understand you correctly, religious education became compulsory in schools for elementary and secondary school-aged children?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Had it been compulsory before?

utterances.speaker: SERGIJA VESELINOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were part of the eastern bloc, where the League of Communists was the ruling party, and any mention of religion was condemned. So the answer to your question would be, no. There was no religious education. As far as I can remember, there was the theory of Marxism --
